results.diagnosis: pandas 3.0 changed pd.offsets.Day to add a calendar day preserving local wall time instead of a fixed 24 h. The code relies on a fixed 24 h step across DST transitions, so the hour shifts on the new version. Replacing the Day offset with a fixed pd.Timedelta(days=n_days) gives an absolute 24 h addition that matches the 2.3.3 behaviour on both versions.

Pandas 3.0 changed `pd.offsets.Day` to preserve local wall-clock time across DST transitions, so adding a calendar day no longer equals an absolute 24 h shift. The golden output requires an absolute elapsed-time addition. Replacing the Day offset with `pd.Timedelta(days=n_days)` makes the addition absolute on both pandas 2.3.3 and 3.0.6, restoring the expected timestamps.

pandas 3.0 changed the semantics of adding a DateOffset to a tz-aware Timestamp from a fixed 24 h absolute shift to a wall-clock calendar shift. The golden output requires the old absolute 24 h behaviour. Using a fixed Timedelta(days=…) restores the absolute shift on both pandas 2.3.3 and 3.0.6, and short-circuiting count==0 avoids constructing an out-of-bounds Timestamp for the generated edge case.

Pandas 3.0 changed the semantics of `pd.offsets.Day` addition on tz-aware timestamps from absolute 24 h to calendar-day wall-time preservation, so `t0 + Day` now keeps the local clock time across DST transitions. The golden output requires absolute 24 h addition. Using `pd.Timedelta(days=n_days)` gives an absolute duration on both pandas 2.3.3 and 3.0.6.

pandas 3.0 changed pd.offsets.Day to perform a calendar-day (wall-time) addition instead of a fixed 24 h addition. Across a DST transition this keeps the local clock hour and changes the UTC offset, giving 12:00 -0400 instead of the expected 13:00 -0400. Using a fixed-duration Timedelta(days=n_days) preserves the absolute 24 h step on both pandas 2.3.3 and 3.0.6.
